Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 1) The route with 100% bioavailability by definition is:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: IV route delivers drug directly into systemic circulation. So absorption is not required. Bioavailability is 100% by definition.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 2) The safest, commonest, most convenient and economical route is:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Oral route is the most common and convenient route. It is also economical and generally safe. But absorption is variable and food may affect it.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 3) Oral route is limited mainly because of variable absorption and:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Oral drugs may undergo first-pass metabolism. This reduces the amount reaching systemic circulation. Food and GI irritation are also important limitations.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 4) Intravenous route is preferred when the desired effect is:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: IV route gives immediate effect. It bypasses absorption barriers. It is useful in emergencies.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 5) Which route is not suitable for oily substances?
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: IV route is not suitable for oily substances. Asepsis is essential. Some drugs must also be given slowly.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 6) Subcutaneous aqueous solution usually gives:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: SC absorption depends on diluent. Aqueous solution gives prompt absorption. Depot preparation gives slower sustained absorption.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 7) Subcutaneous depot preparation is useful for:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: SC route can be used for slow-release preparations. Depot preparations provide sustained absorption. Large volumes and irritating drugs are unsuitable.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 8) Intramuscular route is especially suitable for:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.option1: Drugs needing complete avoidance of absorption
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.option2: Highly irritant drugs in huge volume
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: IM route can be used for oily vehicles. It can handle moderate volumes. Depot IM injections may provide sustained release.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 9) Intramuscular injection should be used carefully in patients on anticoagulants because of risk of:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: IM injection may cause bleeding into muscle. This risk increases during anticoagulant therapy. Alternative routes may be safer when possible.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 10) Transdermal patches usually give:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Transdermal patches provide slow, sustained delivery. They bypass first-pass metabolism. They are useful for prolonged action.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 11) Drugs suitable for transdermal patches should usually be:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Transdermal absorption needs passage through skin. Highly lipophilic drugs cross skin better. Only limited drugs and doses are suitable.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 12) Rectal route is useful when the patient has:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Rectal route may be useful if oral intake is not possible. Vomiting is a common indication. Absorption is erratic and variable.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 13) Rectal route bypasses first-pass metabolism:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Rectal route partly bypasses first-pass metabolism. It does not avoid it completely. Absorption is also variable.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 14) Inhalation route gives rapid systemic absorption especially for:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Inhalation gives rapid systemic absorption for gases. It can also produce local action in lungs. Dose regulation may be difficult.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 15) Inhaled local therapy for lung disease has the advantage of:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Inhaled therapy can act locally in lungs. This reduces systemic exposure. It is useful in asthma and COPD.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 16) Sublingual route is useful because it:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Sublingual drugs enter systemic circulation directly. They bypass first-pass metabolism and stomach acid. Only selected drugs are suitable.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 17) Sublingual GTN is useful because it avoids:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: GTN undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism orally. Sublingual route bypasses this effect. It gives rapid direct systemic absorption.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 18) A disadvantage of sublingual route is:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.option2: Drug may be lost if swallowed
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Sublingual drug must remain under the tongue. If swallowed, it may lose benefit of first-pass avoidance. Taste issue is another limitation.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 19) Bioavailability means fraction of administered drug reaching systemic circulation in:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Bioavailability is the fraction reaching systemic circulation unchanged. IV route has complete bioavailability. Oral bioavailability varies widely.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 20) First-pass metabolism usually:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: First-pass metabolism occurs before drug reaches systemic circulation. It reduces unchanged drug availability. This is important for many oral drugs.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 21) The route with most rapid onset and complete bioavailability is:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: IV route bypasses absorption. It gives immediate effect. Its bioavailability is 100%.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 22) Oral bioavailability may range approximately from:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Oral bioavailability is highly variable. It depends on absorption and first-pass metabolism. Dosage form and disease state may also affect it.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 23) Intramuscular bioavailability is approximately:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: IM bioavailability is usually 75–100%. Absorption depends on formulation and blood supply. Depot preparations may delay absorption.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 24) Subcutaneous bioavailability is approximately:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: SC bioavailability is usually 75–100%. Aqueous solutions are absorbed more promptly. Depot preparations act slowly.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 25) Rectal bioavailability is approximately:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Rectal bioavailability is variable. It may partly avoid first-pass metabolism. Absorption may be erratic.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 26) Transdermal bioavailability is approximately:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Transdermal route has high bioavailability for suitable drugs. It avoids first-pass metabolism. Absorption is slow and prolonged.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 27) Which factor can affect bioavailability?
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Particle size can influence dissolution and absorption. Drug form, disintegration time and dissolution time also matter. These affect the amount reaching systemic circulation.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 28) Disintegration time and dissolution time mainly influence:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: A drug must disintegrate and dissolve before absorption. Poor dissolution may reduce bioavailability. This is especially important for oral preparations.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 29) High first-pass metabolism is seen with:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: GTN undergoes high first-pass metabolism. This is why sublingual administration is useful. Propranolol, verapamil and morphine also show high first-pass metabolism.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 30) Which drug has high first-pass metabolism?
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Verapamil has high first-pass metabolism. This reduces oral bioavailability. Route and dose selection must consider this.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 31) Which opioid has high first-pass metabolism?
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Morphine undergoes significant first-pass metabolism. Oral dose requirements may differ from parenteral dose. Pethidine is also listed among high first-pass drugs.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 32) Plasma protein-bound drug is mainly:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Protein-bound drug acts as storage or inactive form. It undergoes less metabolism while bound. It has delayed onset and longer duration.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 33) Free drug is mainly:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Free drug is pharmacologically active. It can undergo metabolism and excretion. It usually has rapid onset and shorter half-life.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 34) Plasma protein binding usually causes:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Protein-bound drug is slowly released. It is less available for metabolism and excretion. So duration and half-life may increase.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 35) Protein-bound drug usually has:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Bound drug is not immediately active. It must dissociate from protein first. This delays onset compared with free drug.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 36) Which is a classic highly protein-bound drug?
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Warfarin is highly protein-bound. Displacement interactions can increase free drug level. This may increase bleeding risk.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 37) Which drug is highly protein-bound?
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Phenytoin is highly protein-bound. It also has narrow therapeutic range. Small changes in free concentration may matter clinically.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 38) Which sulfonylurea is highly protein-bound?
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Gliclazide is listed among highly protein-bound drugs. Glipizide is also highly protein-bound. Displacement interactions may increase hypoglycaemia risk.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 39) Volume of distribution is best defined as:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.option2: Virtual volume in which drug appears distributed
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Vd is an apparent or virtual volume. It relates amount of drug in body to plasma concentration. It does not necessarily equal a real anatomical volume.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 40) High volume of distribution usually means:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.option2: More tissue binding and less plasma binding
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.option3: More plasma binding and less tissue binding
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: High Vd indicates extensive distribution into tissues. Plasma concentration becomes relatively low. Such drugs often have longer half-life.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 41) Low volume of distribution usually means:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Low Vd means drug stays more in plasma. It usually has more plasma protein binding and less tissue binding. Water-soluble drugs often have lower Vd.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 42) High Vd drugs are generally:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Lipid-soluble drugs distribute widely into tissues. This increases apparent Vd. They are less confined to plasma.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 43) Low Vd drugs are generally:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Water-soluble drugs remain more in plasma and extracellular fluid. They have lower tissue distribution. Therefore Vd is lower.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 44) High Vd is usually associated with:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: High Vd means more tissue storage. Drug returns slowly to plasma for elimination. So half-life is often longer.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 45) Low Vd is usually associated with:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Low Vd drugs remain more in plasma. They are more accessible for elimination. So half-life is usually shorter.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 46) Digoxin is an example of:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Digoxin has high Vd. It distributes extensively into tissues. This contributes to long half-life and toxicity concern.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 47) Gentamicin is an example of:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Gentamicin has low Vd. It is water-soluble and remains more in extracellular fluid. Dose adjustment is important in renal impairment.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 48) Chloroquine is best matched with:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Chloroquine is a high Vd drug. It has extensive tissue distribution. High tissue binding lowers plasma concentration relative to total body amount.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 49) Furosemide is best matched with:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Furosemide is listed as a low Vd drug. Low Vd suggests more plasma confinement. Plasma protein binding is relatively more important.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 50) Which drug is a low Vd example?
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Tobramycin is a low Vd drug. It is an aminoglycoside and remains more in extracellular fluid. This contrasts with lipophilic drugs like imipramine and fluoxetine.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 51) Loading dose is most directly related to:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Loading dose depends mainly on Vd and target plasma concentration. A large Vd usually requires a larger loading dose. Bioavailability must also be considered if the route is not IV. This is important when rapid therapeutic concentration is needed.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 52) Maintenance dose is more directly related to:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Maintenance dose replaces the amount of drug eliminated over time. So it depends mainly on clearance and desired steady concentration. Vd mainly affects loading dose. This distinction is important in dose calculation.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 53) A highly protein-bound drug may cause interaction by:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Highly protein-bound drugs may compete for albumin binding. Displacement can increase free active drug. This may increase toxicity, especially with narrow therapeutic index drugs. Warfarin and phenytoin are classic examples.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 54) A drug with low Vd and high plasma protein binding is likely to remain mainly in:
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Low Vd indicates limited tissue distribution. High plasma protein binding keeps drug in vascular compartment. Plasma concentration remains relatively higher. Such drugs may be more affected by protein-binding displacement.

Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.question: 55) Which statement is most accurate?
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.option2: High Vd means drug remains only in plasma
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.option3: Low Vd means drug is highly tissue-bound
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.option4: Only free drug is pharmacologically active
Routes of drug administration, bioavaila.exp: Free drug can bind receptors and produce action. Protein-bound drug is mainly inactive storage form. Only free drug is available for metabolism and excretion. Changes in free fraction can alter both effect and toxicity.
